subject: sorted out Hessian-vector products for auto-dif

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: sorted out Hessian-vector products for auto-dif
parts:
To lead with the punchline, we can pretty easily and
efficiently implement arbitrary Hessian-vector (or
row vector-Hessian) products in a single pass of efficient
forward auto-dif followed by reverse mode auto-dif of
the result.

Michael and I spent part of his first day talking
about how we could do Hessian-vector products with auto-diff.
He gave me enough hints on the so-called R operator that I could
work out the algebra and auto-dif implementation from scratch.

This will be useful for RM-HMC and for optimizations
using curvature info.

On 12/12/12 4:09 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:

> Efficient Hessian-Vector Products:
>
> Bishop 5.4.6
> http://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/viewdoc/summary?doi=10.1.1.29.6143
> http://justindomke.wordpress.com/2009/01/17/hessian-vector-products/

What helped me the most was the doc for Theano:

http://deeplearning.net/software/theano/tutorial/gradients.html

which presented it in a more computer-sciency way than most of
the other applied math and physics thing I looked at (like Bishop).

I then worked through the algebra and derived the R operator myself,
which is pretty trivial. As an upside, I can now follow the discussion
in Bishop, which I never understood before.

The key is noticing that if H is the Hessian of y w.r.t. x and v
is any old vector, then the first step is noting that:

H * v = grad_x ((grad_x y)' * v)

Then we use a little of the old lambda abstraction to create an
operator:

R = lambda y. [ v' * (grad_x y) ]

so that

R(y) = v' * grad_x y

= v1 * dy/dx1 + v2 * dy/dx2 + ... + vK * dy/dxK

and

H * v = grad_x R(y)

The key to making it efficient in auto-dif is to compute R(y) using
a forward-mode auto dif, then do the outer grad_x using reverse mode
on the result. And the beauty is we only need to implement standard
templated forward-mode auto-dif once in a simple templated way and
we can then use it to do these calculations with the right initializations ---
the adjoint of x_k is initialized to v_k and Bob's your uncle.

The whole calc will probably take on the order of 2 or 3 times the
time for the basic gradient, so about 10 times the cost of the function
eval itself.

I've already implemented most of the basic forward dif, though I pulled
it out of version control ages ago because we weren't using it for anything.

After the next release, I'll pull it back into the main branch and then we
only have to implement gradients for special functions (which is much much
eaiser to do efficiently than reverse mode).

- Bob

messages.author: 1004dd6f66bb10c3
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] sorted out Hessian-vector products for auto-dif
parts:
It's not totally straightforward to do it in linear time. Not insanely
complicated, but not as straightforward as Hessian-vector products.

Basically, I think it winds up looking a lot like reverse-mode AD, but
instead of leveraging
∂/∂x_i f(g(x)) = ∂f/∂g ∂g/∂x_i,
which only involves first derivatives, you have to use
∂^2/∂x_i^2 f(g(x)) = ∂^2 f/∂g^2 (∂g/∂x_i)^2 + ∂f/∂g ∂^2 g/∂x_i^2
which involves a bunch of second derivatives. Those might be
implementable using the Hessian-vector product trick, though.

It'd probably be a reasonable amount of work to implement this, so it
may not be a first-tier priority, but it'd be great to have someday. I
don't think any other autodiff package has the ability to compute
diagonal Hessians in linear time, and it's a useful thing to have
sometimes.

Matt

messages.author: 1004dd6f66bb10c3
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] sorted out Hessian-vector products for auto-dif
parts:
To clarify, when I said "a reasonable amount of work" I meant "a lot of work."

I wonder if an alternative could be found to coding all of the
2nd-order derivatives. We only need them so that we can multiply them
by gradients, which means we don't need to form them explicitly at
all. Maybe there's a way to implement it that only touches the base
vari class.

The connection to variational inference is in my ICML paper with Sam
Gershman, which uses Taylor approximations to do VB, approximating the
posterior with a mixture of isotropic Gaussians:
http://icml.cc/discuss/2012/360.html
The only obstacle to implementing it in Stan is the lack of cheap
diagonal Hessians. I may implement it in Stan soon with the N^2
diagonal Hessian calculation anyway, actually.

Matt

On 12/17/12 6:21 PM, Matt Hoffman wrote:
> To clarify, when I said "a reasonable amount of work" I meant "a lot of work."

I think very different about two kinds of work. The first
is hard work like building a brick wall -- it doesn't need
any technology innovation, but there's lots of hard work.
That's what second-order auto-dif's like.

The other kind of hard work is like that involved in NUTS.
Lots of brain work required first, but then when it's sorted,
not much coding effort.

> I wonder if an alternative could be found to coding all of the
> 2nd-order derivatives. We only need them so that we can multiply them
> by gradients, which means we don't need to form them explicitly at
> all. Maybe there's a way to implement it that only touches the base
> vari class.

So you only need a (diagonal Hessian)-gradient product?
That should be much easier.

Michael B just laid a tensor (third-order derivative) matrix
trace problem on me today, which I think can also be simplified
with auto-dif.

Writing this stuff out in text or on paper is harder than coding
the basic systems. The Hessian calc's only six or seven lines of
code on top of fwd and reverse auto-dif!

> The connection to variational inference is in my ICML paper with Sam
> Gershman, which uses Taylor approximations to do VB, approximating the
> posterior with a mixture of isotropic Gaussians:
> http://icml.cc/discuss/2012/360.html
> The only obstacle to implementing it in Stan is the lack of cheap
> diagonal Hessians. I may implement it in Stan soon with the N^2
> diagonal Hessian calculation anyway, actually.

Cool. We should prioritize getting all the forward-mode auto-difs
done, then. It'll still be 3n or so worse than computing just
the probability function, though.

- Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] sorted out Hessian-vector products for auto-dif
parts:
> So you only need a (diagonal Hessian)-gradient product?
> That should be much easier.
Well, for the diagonal SoftAbs it'd also be nice to have products of the form M . v where v is a vector of second derivatives and M is the gradient of v.

> Michael B just laid a tensor (third-order derivative) matrix
> trace problem on me today, which I think can also be simplified
> with auto-dif.

I was working through this and I'm pretty sure you can do it in O(N^{2}) provided you can compute a dense Hessian (although you'd have to be able to compute the Hessian of autodiff vars instead of doubles).
